1. INTRODUCTION

Electronic financial payments have become the cornerstone of global commerce, processing trillions of dollars across digital point-of-sale terminals, mobile wallets, and e-commerce payment gateways. Concurrently, criminal fraud syndicates have evolved sophisticated attack vectors—including automated credential stuffing, card-not-present (CNP) identity theft, and high-velocity micro-transaction testing. According to global banking security audits, credit card fraud causes tens of billions of dollars in losses annually, directly eroding consumer trust and imposing severe financial reconciliation overhead on banks, payment processors, and merchants.

Traditional fraud prevention architectures rely predominantly on static, rule-based screening systems (e.g., flagging transactions exceeding $5,000, or rejecting cards when multiple transactions originate across different countries within thirty minutes). While such static heuristic filters capture naive fraudulent attempts, they completely fail when faced with adaptive adversary evasion, non-linear fraud patterns, and micro-transaction card testing. Furthermore, as transactional velocity reaches tens of thousands of operations per second, monolithic relational database systems experience extreme computational bottlenecks, causing unacceptable payment processing latency.

This capstone project introduces Financial Transaction Fraud Detection using PySpark, a high-performance distributed machine learning architecture built on Apache Spark and PySpark MLlib. The system leverages distributed Resilient Distributed Datasets (RDDs) and in-memory Spark DataFrames to ingest, preprocess, assemble, scale, and evaluate millions of transactional records in parallel. By uniting cost-sensitive supervised classification models (Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, and Linear Support Vector Machines) with unsupervised distance-based anomaly clustering (K-Means), this platform provides a dual-layer defense against both known fraud signatures and zero-day anomalous attacks.

1.1 Background of the Study

The empirical foundation of modern fraud detection research centers on high-volume card transaction streams characterized by extreme class imbalance. In legitimate real-world operations, only a microscopic fraction of all card swipes represent criminal fraud—typically fewer than 0.2%. The benchmark Kaggle Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset (compiled by the Machine Learning Group at Université Libre de Bruxelles) contains 284,807 card transactions recorded over a two-day span, of which only 492 are fraudulent (an extreme imbalance ratio of 577 to 1).

Three fundamental characteristics define this problem space:

  • Extreme Class Imbalance: Naive machine learning models trained on this data achieve 99.83% accuracy simply by classifying every single transaction as non-fraudulent, yet fail to catch a single criminal dollar. Standard classification metrics like raw accuracy are entirely misleading; the system must optimize for Recall (Sensitivity), Precision, the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (PR-AUC), and the Area Under the ROC Curve (ROC-AUC).
  • Computational Scale & Latency: Real-world banking rails require real-time risk scoring within 50 to 100 milliseconds per transaction, combined with batch processing of daily historical ledgers containing billions of rows. Single-node tools (such as standard Scikit-Learn or Pandas) hit memory bounds and cannot scale across cluster nodes.
  • Information Privacy (PCA Transformed Features): Due to strict customer confidentiality laws (GDPR, PCI-DSS), raw account numbers, merchant names, and geographic coordinates are transformed via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) into latent orthogonal features (V1 through V28), alongside continuous Time and transaction Amount.

1.2 Motivation

The motivation behind this project is twofold:

  • Financial & Operational: Every false negative (a missed fraudulent charge) results in direct monetary theft, chargeback penalties, and potential regulatory liability. Conversely, every false positive (a legitimate customer purchase wrongly blocked at the checkout register) damages user loyalty and drives churn. An enterprise-grade fraud intelligence system must give credit card issuers fine-grained mathematical control over the precision-recall trade-off.
  • Architectural & Technological: Demonstrating that Apache Spark's distributed in-memory data processing paradigm can be cleanly integrated with PySpark MLlib pipelines to solve non-linear classification and unsupervised anomaly detection on massive datasets. The project explores distributed feature normalization (StandardScaler), vectorization (VectorAssembler), and custom cost-sensitive weighted loss functions to counteract severe imbalance without relying on synthetic data fabrication.

1.3 Problem Statement

Modern financial systems face four core challenges:

  • The Imbalance Trap: Standard statistical algorithms assume balanced class distributions. Under a 577:1 imbalance ratio, unweighted algorithms minimize cross-entropy loss by predicting the majority class, resulting in disastrous false-negative rates for fraud.
  • Single-Node Scalability Bottlenecks: Memory exhaustion and CPU saturation occur when single-machine frameworks attempt to ingest and train models on multi-gigabyte financial ledgers.
  • Zero-Day Novel Fraud Blindspots: Supervised models trained exclusively on historical fraud patterns cannot recognize novel, emergent attack vectors that have never been previously labeled.
  • Evaluation Metric Pitfalls: Relying on accuracy rather than ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and cost-benefit confusion matrices conceals catastrophic model failure.

1.4 Objectives

Five measurable, verifiable objectives guide the development of this platform:

  • O1 — Distributed Ingestion & Hygiene: Build an Apache Spark distributed pipeline capable of ingesting high-volume financial transaction records, enforcing typed schemas, confirming zero null/corrupted fields, and maintaining microsecond distributed caching.
  • O2 — Imbalance-Compensating Feature Pipeline: Design a distributed preprocessing pipeline using PySpark's VectorAssembler and StandardScaler that dynamically calculates inverse-class-frequency cost weights (w0 ≈ 0.50, w1 ≈ 289.44), penalizing missed fraud 577x more heavily than false alarms.
  • O3 — Supervised Model Benchmarking: Train, tune, and evaluate three distinct PySpark MLlib classification models: Logistic Regression with elastic-net regularization and cost-sensitive loss, Decision Tree Classifier with entropy/Gini impurity optimization, and Linear Support Vector Machine (LinearSVC) with margin maximization.
  • O4 — Unsupervised Anomaly Exploration: Implement a distributed K-Means clustering model (k=4) that scores transactions by Euclidean distance to the nearest cluster centroid, establishing a 98.5th percentile anomaly threshold to detect zero-day fraud without supervision.
  • O5 — Comprehensive Empirical Evaluation & Visualization: Generate publication-grade comparative visualizations (Confusion Matrices, ROC Curves, Precision-Recall Curves, PCA Cluster Plots, and Feature Importances) and demonstrate simulated real-time stream scoring.

1.5 Overview of the Proposed System

The system is structured as a modular, four-tier distributed pipeline: Ingestion Tier, Feature Engineering Tier, Machine Learning Modeling Tier, and Scoring & Evaluation Tier.

1.6 Scope and Limitations

The scope covers distributed machine learning workflows on numerical financial transaction records, featuring 284,807 transactions. Evaluates three supervised classifiers and one unsupervised detector. The limitations are clearly stated: features V1 to V28 are pre-transformed via PCA, preventing semantic domain feature engineering (such as cardholder billing zip codes or merchant categories). The system operates on batch-distributed processing and simulated streaming.

2. PROFILE OF THE PROBLEM

2.1 Problem Statement

In financial transaction processing, fraudulent transactions represent an adversarial needle in a haystack. While accounting for only 0.172% of total transaction volume, their financial impact is catastrophic. When a fraudulent transaction slips past security, the merchant suffers chargeback fines, the cardholder endures identity theft, and the issuing bank must reimburse the lost funds.

Existing single-node analytic scripts fail when datasets expand beyond system RAM. Furthermore, conventional machine learning models penalize false positives and false negatives equally. In fraud detection, however, a False Negative (allowing a $2,000 stolen-card transaction) is orders of magnitude more damaging than a False Positive (prompting a cardholder for an SMS two-factor verification code). A mathematically rigorous fraud detection architecture must directly incorporate this cost asymmetry into its training objective.

2.2 Rationale and Scope of the Study

The rationale for choosing Apache Spark and PySpark MLlib lies in Spark's memory-centric distributed architecture. By maintaining resilient distributed datasets in RAM across cluster partitions, PySpark delivers training and inference throughput up to 100 times faster than disk-bound MapReduce architectures and eliminates the memory limits of single-node Python libraries.

3.3 System Architecture of Existing Tools

Traditional bank fraud architectures route incoming transactions through a relational transactional database (OLTP) to an external rule engine. When a rule is tripped, an analyst queue ticket is generated. This architecture suffers from three major flaws: I/O disk bottlenecks, static vulnerability, and the equal loss assumption.

3.4 What Is New in This System

  • Native Distributed MLlib Pipeline: Combines VectorAssembler and StandardScaler into a single reproducible pipeline.
  • Cost-Sensitive Asymmetric Loss: Penalizes missed fraud by 289.44x, preventing models from degenerating into trivial zero-predictors.
  • Hybrid Zero-Day Anomaly Detection: Employs K-Means centroid distance to detect unlabelled fraud without supervision.

4. PROBLEM ANALYSIS

4.1 Product Definition

AquaLens-style intelligence platform: The system delivers automated distributed batch model training, evaluation, anomaly distance thresholding, and real-time transaction screening that outputs triage decisions (e.g., APPROVE vs BLOCK).

4.2 Feasibility Analysis

  • Technical Feasibility: Confirmed. The entire pipeline runs on Apache Spark 3.5.3, PySpark, Python 3.10, and Java 8 SE Runtime. Spark's in-memory execution engine easily accommodates the 284,807 transactions on local multi-core threads and can be seamlessly scaled to an AWS EMR or Databricks multi-node cluster without modifying code.
  • Operational Feasibility: Confirmed. The pipeline is fully automated and self-contained. Analysts can execute end-to-end training and evaluation through a single terminal command or explore interactively through a clean Jupyter Notebook.
  • Economic Feasibility: Outstanding. Zero software licensing fees by leveraging the open-source Apache Spark and Python ecosystem.

6. DESIGN

6.1 System Design

The system follows a four-tier distributed pipeline: Ingestion, Feature Pipeline, Model Training, and Evaluation/Inference.

6.2 Data Pipeline Design

The schema comprises 31 attributes: Time, V1 through V28 (PCA orthogonal projections), Amount, and Class. All 30 continuous features are assembled into a dense vector via VectorAssembler and normalized to zero mean and unit variance via StandardScaler.

6.3 Algorithmic Model Specifications

  1. Logistic Regression: Cost-sensitive weighted log-loss optimization with L2 regularization.
  2. Decision Tree Classifier: Recursive partitioning based on Gini Impurity with max depth 7.
  3. Linear Support Vector Machine (LinearSVC): Soft-margin hinge loss optimization with cost-sensitive class weights.
  4. K-Means Anomaly Scorer: Unsupervised 4-cluster centroid partition scoring each point by Euclidean distance. Transactions exceeding the 98.5th percentile distance (τ = 12.1889) are flagged as anomalies.

Detecting fraud requires: 1. High-throughput distributed processing capable of handling millions of real-time transactions. 2. In this project, we architect and evaluate an end-to-end distributed machine learning system using **PySpark SQL** and **MLlib**, comparing **Logistic Regression**, **Decision Trees**, **Linear Support Vector Machines (LinearSVC)**, and **K-Means Anomaly Scoring**.

--- ## 4. Feature Engineering & Class Imbalance Mitigation To address the severe 577:1 class imbalance without synthetic data distortion: 1. **Cost-Sensitive Weighting:** We assign inverse class frequency weights to the loss function (`weight_fraud = total / (2 * fraud_count)`), penalizing missed fraud 577x more heavily than false alarms. 2. **Feature Assembly (`VectorAssembler`):** Combining all 30 input columns `[V1..V28, Amount, Time]` into a feature vector. 3. **Feature Standardization (`StandardScaler`):** Normalizing all features to mean 0 and unit variance.
In [5]:
feature_cols = [f"V{i}" for i in range(1, 29)] + ["Amount", "Time"]

# Calculate balanced class weights
weight_fraud = total_rows / (2.0 * fraud_count)
weight_legit = total_rows / (2.0 * legit_count)
print(f"Cost-Sensitive Loss Weights -> Legit (0): {weight_legit:.4f} | Fraud (1): {weight_fraud:.4f}")

df_weighted = df.withColumn(
    "weight",
    F.when(F.col("Class") == 1, weight_fraud).otherwise(weight_legit)
)

assembler = VectorAssembler(inputCols=feature_cols, outputCol="raw_features")
scaler = StandardScaler(inputCol="raw_features", outputCol="scaled_features", withMean=True, withStd=True)

# Train-Test Partitioning (80% Train, 20% Test, Seed 42)
train_df, test_df = df_weighted.randomSplit([0.8, 0.2], seed=42)
train_df = train_df.cache()
test_df = test_df.cache()

print(f"Training Set:   {train_df.count():,} rows")
print(f"Testing Set:    {test_df.count():,} rows")

# Fit Feature Pipeline on Training Set only (preventing data leakage)
feature_pipeline = Pipeline(stages=[assembler, scaler])
feature_model = feature_pipeline.fit(train_df)

train_prepared = feature_model.transform(train_df).cache()
test_prepared = feature_model.transform(test_df).cache()
print("Feature preparation complete!")

--- ## 5. Supervised Model Training & Evaluation We train three diverse classification paradigms on Apache Spark: 1. **Logistic Regression** (Linear baseline with cost-sensitive weighted loss). 2. **Decision Tree Classifier** (Non-linear recursive partitioning). 3. **Linear Support Vector Machine (LinearSVC)** (Max-margin hyper-plane with cost-sensitive weights).
In [6]:
eval_roc = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="Class", rawPredictionCol="rawPrediction", metricName="areaUnderROC")
eval_pr = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="Class", rawPredictionCol="rawPrediction", metricName="areaUnderPR")

def compute_metrics(predictions, pred_col="prediction"):
    tp = predictions.filter(f"Class == 1 AND {pred_col} == 1.0").count()
    fp = predictions.filter(f"Class == 0 AND {pred_col} == 1.0").count()
    tn = predictions.filter(f"Class == 0 AND {pred_col} == 0.0").count()
    fn = predictions.filter(f"Class == 1 AND {pred_col} == 0.0").count()
    
    total = tp + fp + tn + fn
    acc = (tp + tn) / total
    prec = tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) > 0 else 0.0
    rec = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * (prec * rec) / (prec + rec) if (prec + rec) > 0 else 0.0
    
    return {"TP": tp, "FP": fp, "TN": tn, "FN": fn, "Accuracy": acc, "Precision": prec, "Recall": rec, "F1": f1}

results = {}
In [7]:
# 1. Logistic Regression
print("Fitting Logistic Regression (Weighted Loss)...")
lr = LogisticRegression(featuresCol="scaled_features", labelCol="Class", weightCol="weight", maxIter=30, regParam=0.01)
t0 = time.time()
lr_model = lr.fit(train_prepared)
lr_time = time.time() - t0

lr_preds = lr_model.transform(test_prepared).cache()
m_lr = compute_metrics(lr_preds)
m_lr["ROC_AUC"] = eval_roc.evaluate(lr_preds)
m_lr["PR_AUC"] = eval_pr.evaluate(lr_preds)
m_lr["Train_Time_s"] = lr_time
results["Logistic Regression"] = m_lr

print(f"Logistic Regression ({lr_time:.2f}s): Recall={m_lr['Recall']:.4f}, Precision={m_lr['Precision']:.4f}, F1={m_lr['F1']:.4f}, ROC-AUC={m_lr['ROC_AUC']:.4f}")

--- ## 6. Unsupervised Anomaly Exploration with K-Means In cold-start environments or zero-day fraud scenarios where fraud labels are not yet available, unsupervised anomaly detection is essential. We train a distributed **K-Means Clustering** model ($k=4$), compute the Euclidean distance of each transaction to its cluster centroid, and flag transactions exceeding the 98.5th percentile distance threshold as anomalous.
In [10]:
print("Fitting K-Means Clustering for Anomaly Scoring...")
kmeans = KMeans(featuresCol="scaled_features", predictionCol="cluster", k=4, seed=42, maxIter=20)
t0 = time.time()
km_model = kmeans.fit(train_prepared)
km_time = time.time() - t0

centers = [np.array(c) for c in km_model.clusterCenters()]
centers_bc = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(centers)

def get_dist(cluster_id, vec):
    c = centers_bc.value[int(cluster_id)]
    return float(np.linalg.norm(np.array(vec.toArray()) - c))

dist_udf = F.udf(get_dist, DoubleType())

km_train = km_model.transform(train_prepared).withColumn("dist_to_center", dist_udf(F.col("cluster"), F.col("scaled_features")))
km_test = km_model.transform(test_prepared).withColumn("dist_to_center", dist_udf(F.col("cluster"), F.col("scaled_features"))).cache()

# Compute 98.5th percentile threshold on training baseline
threshold = km_train.stat.approxQuantile("dist_to_center", [0.985], 0.001)[0]
print(f"Unsupervised Anomaly Distance Cutoff (98.5%): {threshold:.4f}")

km_test = km_test.withColumn("anomaly_pred", F.when(F.col("dist_to_center") >= threshold, 1.0).otherwise(0.0)).cache()
m_km = compute_metrics(km_test, pred_col="anomaly_pred")

eval_roc_dist = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="Class", rawPredictionCol="dist_to_center", metricName="areaUnderROC")
eval_pr_dist = BinaryClassificationEvaluator(labelCol="Class", rawPredictionCol="dist_to_center", metricName="areaUnderPR")

m_km["ROC_AUC"] = eval_roc_dist.evaluate(km_test)
m_km["PR_AUC"] = eval_pr_dist.evaluate(km_test)
m_km["Train_Time_s"] = km_time
results["K-Means Anomaly Detector"] = m_km

print(f"K-Means Anomaly ({km_time:.2f}s): Recall={m_km['Recall']:.4f}, Precision={m_km['Precision']:.4f}, F1={m_km['F1']:.4f}, ROC-AUC={m_km['ROC_AUC']:.4f}")
Out [10]:

K-Means Anomaly (8.03s): Recall=0.6699, Precision=0.0756, F1=0.1358, ROC-AUC=0.9407

--- ## 9. Real-Time Transaction Screening Simulation Demonstrating real-time batch transaction scoring using the trained PySpark MLlib models.
In [13]:
# Sample 5 fraudulent transactions and 5 legitimate transactions from test set
sample_fraud = test_prepared.filter("Class == 1").limit(5)
sample_legit = test_prepared.filter("Class == 0").limit(5)
sample_stream = sample_fraud.union(sample_legit)

scored_stream = lr_model.transform(sample_stream).select(
    "Time", "Amount", "Class",
    vector_to_array("probability")[1].alias("Fraud_Probability"),
    "prediction"
).withColumn(
    "Decision",
    F.when(F.col("prediction") == 1.0, "ALERT: HIGH RISK FRAUD - BLOCK").otherwise("APPROVE TRANSACTION")
).toPandas()

print("Real-Time Transaction Scoring Output:")
display(scored_stream)

--- ## 10. Conclusion & Architectural Insights 1. **Recall vs Precision Trade-off:** In banking, missing a fraud transaction incurs substantial financial losses and chargebacks. Logistic Regression and Linear SVM with class-weighted loss achieve over **82.5% Recall** (ROC-AUC > 0.975), capturing the vast majority of frauds. 2. **Precision Leader:** Decision Tree achieves **80.9% Precision** with only 17 false alarms, making it well-suited when minimizing customer verification friction is the primary operational objective. 3. **Unsupervised Utility:** K-Means clustering successfully flags **67.0% of fraud transactions** purely by measuring geometric outlier distance in feature space, proving its value as a zero-day screening layer. 4. **PySpark Scalability:** Spark's distributed architecture enabled reading, preprocessing, scaling, and training 4 models on 284,807 transactions in seconds, validating its production suitability for high-velocity payment rails.
